name: Bell-LaPadula access-control decisions and label lattice
theory_paragraphs: Some organizations (military, intelligence, companies with trade secrets) classify information at several levels of sensitivity, and want a guarantee that information can never flow from a more sensitive place to a less sensitive one. Such a system is called a \term{multilevel security (MLS)} system. In it, every \term{subject} (an active entity: a user, or a process running on a user's behalf) and every \term{object} (a passive container of information: a file, a record) carries a \term{security label}. The subject's label is called its \term{clearance}, the object's label its \term{classification}. A label is a pair $L = (SL, C)$: a \term{sensitivity level} $SL$ taken from an ordered list (for example Unclassified $<$ Confidential $<$ Secret $<$ Top Secret, abbreviated $U < C < S < TS$), and a set of \term{compartments} $C$, which represent topic areas (e.g. \{Nuclear, Crypto\}) and enforce \term{need-to-know}: being cleared for Secret is not enough, you must also be authorized for the specific topic.

Labels are compared by the \term{dominance} relation. We say $L_1 = (SL_1, C_1)$ is dominated by $L_2 = (SL_2, C_2)$, written $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$, if and only if \imp{both} of the following hold: (1) $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ in the level order, and (2) $C_1 \subseteq C_2$, i.e. every compartment of $L_1$ is also a compartment of $L_2$. The reason both conditions are required: being at least as sensitive means being at least as high in the hierarchy \emph{and} covering at least the same topics. Dominance is only a \term{partial order}, not a total one: two labels can be \term{incomparable}, meaning neither dominates the other. This happens when the levels are unordered (some exams use incomparable levels, e.g. $C$ and $S$ both below $TS$ but not related to each other) or when each compartment set contains an element the other lacks, e.g. $\{A, B\}$ versus $\{A, G\}$. With incomparable labels \imp{neither read nor write is allowed}. The set of all labels with dominance forms a \term{lattice}: a bottom element (lowest level, empty compartment set), a top element (highest level, all compartments), and a unique least upper bound and greatest lower bound for every pair.

\term{Bell--LaPadula (BLP)} is a \term{mandatory access control (MAC)} model: access is decided by a fixed central policy, not by the owner of the file (that would be \term{discretionary} access control). BLP enforces two rules that together guarantee information never flows downward. \term{No read up} (the \term{simple security property}, ss-property): subject $s$ may \emph{read} object $o$ iff $f_o(o) \sqsubseteq f_s(s)$ --- the object's label must be dominated by the subject's clearance. In words: you may only read things at your own level or below, and only in compartments you are authorized for. \term{No write down} (the \term{star property}, $*$-property): subject $s$ may \emph{write} object $o$ iff $f_c(s) \sqsubseteq f_o(o)$ --- the subject's label must be dominated by the object's. In words: you may only write things at your own level or above. Writing \emph{up} is deliberately allowed (a Secret user may deposit a report into a Top Secret file it cannot read --- a \term{blind write}); writing \emph{down} is forbidden, because otherwise a Secret user (or a \term{Trojan horse} program running with that user's rights) could copy secret data into an unclassified file where anyone can read it.

Access \term{modes} matter and are a classic exam trap. \term{Read} is checked by the ss-property only; \term{append} is \term{write-only} (add content without seeing the file) and is checked by the $*$-property alone --- so appending \emph{up} is allowed even when reading the same file is denied. If the model states that \term{write implies read}, then a write request must satisfy \emph{both} rules. Some exams tabulate two clearances per subject: the \term{maximum clearance} $f_s(s)$ (the highest the subject is allowed to go) and the \term{current clearance} $f_c(s)$ (the level the session currently runs at, chosen $\leq$ the maximum). Reads are checked against $f_s$, writes against $f_c$; using the wrong one flips verdicts. Finally, declassification or sanitization (legitimately moving data down) is impossible under the two rules and requires \term{trusted subjects} that are exempt --- mention this only if asked about the model's limits.

When a problem asks you to \term{draw the partial order} (Hasse diagram) of the labels: the nodes are all (level, compartment-set) pairs that exist in the system; draw an upward edge from $(SL_1, C_1)$ to $(SL_2, C_2)$ whenever $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$ and no label lies strictly in between (raise the level one step keeping compartments fixed, or add exactly one compartment keeping the level fixed). The bottom of the diagram is (lowest level, $\emptyset$) and the top is (highest level, all compartments). When a problem asks you to \term{invent example labels} achieving a target verdict, run dominance in reverse: for read allowed, make the object's level $\leq$ the subject's and the object's compartments a subset of the subject's; for write allowed do the opposite; for a denial, break one of the two conjuncts (or make labels incomparable).
theory_cheatsheet: Label $L = (SL, C)$; dominance $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ AND $C_1 \subseteq C_2$ --- \imp{both conjuncts must hold}.
\imp{No read up (ss-property):} $s$ reads $o$ iff $f_o(o) \sqsubseteq f_s(s)$ (object dominated by subject).
\imp{No write down (*-property):} $s$ writes $o$ iff $f_c(s) \sqsubseteq f_o(o)$ (subject dominated by object).
Write-up (blind write) is legal; write-down is the leak BLP forbids; append = write-only, only the $*$-property.
\imp{Incomparable labels} (levels unordered, or compartment sets overlapping without inclusion) $\Rightarrow$ \imp{neither read nor write}.
No compartments stated $\Rightarrow$ dominance is just the linear level order; max vs current clearance: read uses $f_s$, write uses $f_c$.
identify_givens: A BLP system stated as: an ordered (or partially ordered) set of sensitivity levels (e.g. $U < C < S < TS$), optionally a set of compartments, the label form $L = (SL, C)$ with dominance $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ and $C_1 \subseteq C_2$, and concrete subject clearances $f_s$/$f_c$ and object classifications $f_o$ (tables or bullet lists). Access modes read, write (may imply read), append (write-only).
identify_target: Formally define no-read-up (ss-property) and no-write-down (*-property); decide grant/deny for each listed (subject, object, mode) request with justification naming the violated rule; possibly draw the label partial order or invent example labels achieving a specified allowed/denied read/write combination.
strategy_name: Dominate-and-decide: formalize the two rules, then check dominance for each request

algorithm.detail: State the label order: for $L_1 = (SL_1, C_1)$ and $L_2 = (SL_2, C_2)$, $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ (level order) and $C_1 \subseteq C_2$ (compartment subset). \imp{Both conjuncts must hold.} If the problem has no compartments, dominance is just $SL_1 \leq SL_2$. Check whether the level order is linear or has incomparable levels.

Write out the concrete label of every subject and object from the tables, e.g. User 1: $(S, \{A, B\})$, File D: $(U, \{\})$. If both maximum clearance $f_s$ and current clearance $f_c$ are given, note which one each rule uses ($f_s$ for read, $f_c$ for write).

For each request state grant or deny plus the exact reason: which dominance holds or fails, and in case of denial name the violated rule (no read up / ss-property, or no write down / $*$-property). \imp{Incomparable labels: neither read nor write.}

Drawing the partial order: nodes are all (level, compartment-set) pairs; edges raise the level one step with the same compartments, or add one compartment with the same level; bottom is (lowest level, $\emptyset$), top is (highest level, all compartments). Inventing labels for a target outcome: run dominance in reverse --- pick levels ordered as required and compartments as subset/superset (allowed) or incomparable sets (denied).

variations.name: Compartments vs no compartments
variations.detail: The HT2018 instance explicitly drops compartments (dominance = linear level order, incomparability impossible); newer exams add compartments, where the trap is comparing only levels and forgetting $C_1 \subseteq C_2$: equal or ordered levels with incomparable compartment sets (e.g. $(S, \{A,B\})$ vs $(S, \{G\})$) mean neither read nor write. Always check both components.

variations.name: Incomparable sensitivity levels
variations.detail: The re-exam uses levels $P < C < TS$ and $P < S < TS$, so $C$ and $S$ are incomparable. A user at $(C, \{A,I\})$ and an object at $(S, \{A,I\})$ cannot read or write in either direction \emph{even though the compartment sets are equal} --- the level comparison alone already fails both ways. Never assume the levels form a single chain.

variations.name: Mode trap: append and write-implies-read
variations.detail: Append (write-only) up is allowed via the $*$-property even though a read would be denied --- the trap is refusing append because read fails (HT2018: Carol may append the Secret file budget). But append still needs full dominance: a high enough level does not rescue a failing compartment set. Conversely, if the stated model lets write imply read, a write request must satisfy both rules.

variations.name: Max vs current clearance
variations.detail: When both $f_s$ (max) and $f_c$ (current) are tabulated (HT2018: Bob max Secret, current Confidential), using the wrong function flips verdicts --- Bob's write to the Secret file budget is denied because $f_c(\text{Bob}) \not\sqsubseteq f_o(\text{budget})$ even though $f_s$ would allow it. Read the problem's convention before deciding.

walkthrough_problem: A freight-rail operator protects infrastructure data with Bell--LaPadula. Sensitivity levels are $U < R < C < S < TS$ (Unclassified, Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) and compartments are $\{N, E, W, K\}$ (the four lines North, East, West, Kargo). Subject clearances: Dispatcher Farah: $(S, \{N, E\})$; Auditor Bjorck: $(C, \{N, W\})$; Technician Osei: $(R, \{N\})$. Object classifications: Dossier: $(C, \{N, E\})$; Blueprint: $(TS, \{N, E, K\})$; Archive: $(C, \{N, W\})$; Log: $(C, \{N\})$; Bulletin: $(U, \{\})$. (a) Formally define the BLP properties \emph{no read up} and \emph{no write down}. (b) For each of the following, decide with justification whether access is granted or denied: Farah reads or writes Dossier and Blueprint; Bjorck reads or writes Archive and Dossier; Osei reads or writes Log and Bulletin. (c) Taking \emph{append} to be write-only: may Bjorck append to Blueprint? May Osei append to Blueprint? Justify.

walkthrough_steps.work: Dominance: $L_1 = (SL_1, C_1) \sqsubseteq L_2 = (SL_2, C_2)$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ \emph{and} $C_1 \subseteq C_2$, with levels $U < R < C < S < TS$ and compartment sets $C_i \subseteq \{N, E, W, K\}$. \textbf{Beginner note:} the single most common error is checking only the level and forgetting the compartment subset. Write both tests down for every request before deciding.

(a) No read up (ss-property): subject $s$ may read object $o$ iff $f_o(o) \sqsubseteq f_s(s)$. No write down ($*$-property): $s$ may write $o$ iff $f_c(s) \sqsubseteq f_o(o)$. Append is write-only, so it needs only the $*$-property. \textbf{Beginner note:} the direction of $\sqsubseteq$ is the second most common error. Memory hook: \imp{read down, write up} --- for a read, the \emph{object} must be the smaller label; for a write, the \emph{subject} must be the smaller label.

Farah $= (S, \{N,E\})$; Bjorck $= (C, \{N,W\})$; Osei $= (R, \{N\})$; Dossier $= (C, \{N,E\})$; Blueprint $= (TS, \{N,E,K\})$; Archive $= (C, \{N,W\})$; Log $= (C, \{N\})$; Bulletin $= (U, \{\})$. \textbf{Beginner note:} write these pairs out explicitly; deciding directly from the prose invites slips. Only one clearance per subject here, so $f_s = f_c$ for everyone.

Farah vs Dossier: read needs $L_{\text{Dos}} \sqsubseteq L_{\text{Farah}}$: $C \leq S$ true, $\{N,E\} \subseteq \{N,E\}$ true --- granted. Write needs $L_{\text{Farah}} \sqsubseteq L_{\text{Dos}}$: $S \leq C$ false --- denied (no write down). Result: read-only. Farah vs Blueprint: read needs $TS \leq S$ --- false, denied (no read up). Write needs $S \leq TS$ true and $\{N,E\} \subseteq \{N,E,K\}$ true --- granted: a \term{blind write} up. Result: write-only. \textbf{Beginner note:} a Secret subject writing a Top Secret file feels wrong to many students; it is exactly the case BLP allows, because information flows up, not down.

Bjorck vs Archive: labels equal, $(C, \{N,W\}) \sqsubseteq (C, \{N,W\})$ in both directions ($C \leq C$ and $\{N,W\} \subseteq \{N,W\}$) --- read and write both granted. \textbf{Beginner note:} equality counts as dominance in both directions ($\leq$, not $<$). Bjorck vs Dossier: read needs $\{N,E\} \subseteq \{N,W\}$ --- false ($E$ missing); write needs $\{N,W\} \subseteq \{N,E\}$ --- false ($W$ missing); the levels are equal but the compartment sets are \term{incomparable}, so neither read nor write. Osei vs Log: read needs $C \leq R$ --- false, denied (no read up); write needs $R \leq C$ and $\{N\} \subseteq \{N\}$ --- granted (write-up). Result: write-only. Osei vs Bulletin: read needs $U \leq R$ and $\{\} \subseteq \{N\}$ --- granted; write needs $R \leq U$ --- false, denied (no write down). Result: read-only.

(c) Append needs only the $*$-property. Bjorck append Blueprint: $(C, \{N,W\}) \sqsubseteq (TS, \{N,E,K\})$ requires $\{N,W\} \subseteq \{N,E,K\}$, which fails since $W \notin \{N,E,K\}$ --- denied, even though $C \leq TS$. \textbf{Beginner note:} the level test passes but the compartment test fails; one failed conjunct kills the whole dominance. Osei append Blueprint: $(R, \{N\}) \sqsubseteq (TS, \{N,E,K\})$ since $R \leq TS$ and $\{N\} \subseteq \{N,E,K\}$ --- granted: a blind write; Osei still may not read Blueprint. Final verdicts: Farah: Dossier read-only, Blueprint write-only; Bjorck: Archive read and write, Dossier neither; Osei: Log write-only, Bulletin read-only; appends: Bjorck denied, Osei granted.

exam_questions.problem: Bell--LaPadula. The system state is $(b, f, H)$, where $b$ is the set of active accesses (triples (subject, object, access mode), modes: read, write (implies read), execute, append (write-only)); $f_s(s)$ is the max security clearance of subject $s$, $f_c(s)$ the current clearance, $f_o(o)$ the classification of object $o$; $H$ is the hierarchy of levels. There is no discretionary access control and no compartments. Level hierarchy: $H$: top secret $>$ secret $>$ confidential $>$ unclassified. Subjects: Alice: $f_s = f_c = $ top secret; Bob: $f_s = $ secret, $f_c = $ confidential; Carol: $f_s = f_c = $ confidential. Objects (files): plan: top secret; budget: secret; rumors: confidential; official: unclassified. Currently active accesses: $b = \{$(Alice, plan, write), (Bob, rumors, read)$\}$. Decide for each access request whether it should be granted, and formally state which BLP rule is violated in case access is denied: (1) Alice, rumors, read; (2) Alice, official, write; (3) Bob, budget, write; (4) Carol, budget, append.

solution_steps.work: No compartments, so dominance is just the level order: $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ in top secret $>$ secret $>$ confidential $>$ unclassified. No read up (ss-property): $s$ reads $o$ iff $f_o(o) \sqsubseteq f_s(s)$. No write down ($*$-property): $s$ writes $o$ iff $f_c(s) \sqsubseteq f_o(o)$. Append is write-only, so it is checked by the $*$-property alone.
Note the trap: Bob has \emph{max} clearance secret but \emph{current} clearance confidential. Writes are checked against $f_c$, reads against $f_s$.
Alice, rumors, read: test $f_o(\text{rumors}) \sqsubseteq f_s(\text{Alice})$, i.e. confidential $\leq$ top secret --- true. \imp{Allow} (ss-property satisfied).

Alice, official, write: test $f_c(\text{Alice}) \sqsubseteq f_o(\text{official})$, i.e. top secret $\leq$ unclassified --- false. \imp{Deny}; the violated rule is the $*$-property (no write down): a top-secret subject may not write an unclassified file.

Bob, budget, write: test $f_c(\text{Bob}) \sqsubseteq f_o(\text{budget})$, i.e. confidential $\leq$ secret --- false (the official solution states $f_c(\text{Bob}) \neq f_o(\text{budget})$). \imp{Deny} by the $*$-property. Had we wrongly used Bob's max clearance $f_s(\text{Bob}) = $ secret, we would have allowed it --- that is the intended trap.

Carol, budget, append: append is write-only, so only the $*$-property applies: $f_c(\text{Carol}) \sqsubseteq f_o(\text{budget})$, i.e. confidential $\leq$ secret --- true. \imp{Allow}: a blind write-up, even though Carol could not read budget.

exam_questions.answer: 1 allow (ss-property); 2 deny (*-property, no write down); 3 deny (*-property, current clearance confidential below secret); 4 allow (*-property, blind append-up).

exam_questions.source: Exam (with solutions), Problem 3a-3b, Access Control - BLP Model
exam_questions.problem: A defense organization uses BLP. Labels are pairs $L = (SL, C)$ of sensitivity levels and compartments, enforcing no read up and no write down. Four clearance levels: Top Secret ($TS$), Secret ($S$), Confidential ($C$), Unclassified ($U$) with $U < C < S < TS$. Three compartments: Alpha ($A$), Beta ($B$), Gamma ($G$). (3a) Define the no read up and no write down rules for a user $U$ with label $L_U = (SL_U, C_U)$ and a file $F$ with label $L_F = (SL_F, C_F)$; give example labels for a user/file pair such that read access is allowed, and example labels such that write access is allowed. (3b) Given User 1: Secret, compartments $\{A, B\}$; User 2: Confidential, compartment $\{G\}$; File A: Top Secret, $\{A, B\}$; File B: Secret, $\{G\}$; File C: Confidential, $\{A\}$; File D: Unclassified, no compartments --- decide for each of the following, with justification, whether the user can read or write the file: User 1 vs File A; User 1 vs File B; User 1 vs File D; User 2 vs File A; User 2 vs File B; User 2 vs File C.

solution_steps.work: No read up: $U$ may read $F$ iff $L_F \sqsubseteq L_U$. No write down: $U$ may write $F$ iff $L_U \sqsubseteq L_F$, where $L_1 = (SL_1, C_1) \sqsubseteq L_2 = (SL_2, C_2)$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ and $C_1 \subseteq C_2$, with $C_i \subseteq \{A, B, G\}$. Example where read is allowed: $L_U = (TS, \{A\})$, $L_F = (S, \{A\})$ (subject level higher, compartments cover the file's). Example where write is allowed: $L_{U1} = (S, \{A\})$, $L_{F1} = (TS, \{A\})$ (blind write-up).

exam_questions.answer: 3a: read iff $L_F \sqsubseteq L_U$, write iff $L_U \sqsubseteq L_F$; read example $(TS,\{A\})$ / $(S,\{A\})$, write example $(S,\{A\})$ / $(TS,\{A\})$. 3b: U1-A write only; U1-B neither; U1-D read only; U2-A neither; U2-B write only; U2-C neither.

exam_questions.source: Re-exam (with sample solutions), Problem 2b, Access Control - BLP Model
exam_questions.problem: An organization uses BLP with labels $L = (SL, C)$. Clearance levels: Top Secret ($TS$), Secret ($S$), Confidential ($C$), Public ($P$), with $P < C < TS$ and $P < S < TS$ (note: $C$ and $S$ are \emph{not} comparable). Two compartments: Academia ($A$) and Industry ($I$). (Part 2a asked for the definitions of no read up / no write down and a drawing of the label partial order.) Problem 2b: (1) Consider a user $U$ with label $L_U = (C, \{A, I\})$ and an object $O$ with label $L_O = (S, \{A, I\})$. Justify whether $U$ can read $O$ and whether $U$ can write $O$. (2-5) Provide example labels for a user $U$ and an object $O$ such that: (2) $U$ is allowed to read $O$; (3) $U$ is not allowed to read $O$; (4) $U$ is allowed to write $O$; (5) $U$ is not allowed to write $O$.

solution_steps.work: No read up: $U$ may read $O$ iff $L_O \sqsubseteq L_U$. No write down: $U$ may write $O$ iff $L_U \sqsubseteq L_O$, where $L_1 = (SL_1, C_1) \sqsubseteq L_2 = (SL_2, C_2)$ iff $SL_1 \leq SL_2$ and $C_1 \subseteq C_2$, with $C_1, C_2 \subseteq \{A, I\}$ and $SL_1, SL_2 \in \{TS, S, C, P\}$. The partial order to draw: an arrow from $L_1$ to $L_2$ whenever $L_1 \sqsubseteq L_2$; because $C$ and $S$ are incomparable, the diagram has two parallel chains $P < C < TS$ and $P < S < TS$.

Read test: $L_O \sqsubseteq L_U$ would need $S \leq C$, but $S$ and $C$ are not comparable, so the level conjunct fails. Write test: $L_U \sqsubseteq L_O$ would need $C \leq S$, which fails for the same reason. Hence $L_U \not\sqsubseteq L_O$ and $L_O \not\sqsubseteq L_U$ --- the labels are incomparable, so user $U$ can \imp{neither read nor write} object $O$, even though the compartment sets $\{A, I\}$ are identical.

(2) Read allowed: $L_U = (S, \{I\})$, $L_O = (P, \{I\})$: $P \leq S$ and $\{I\} \subseteq \{I\}$, so $L_O \sqsubseteq L_U$. (3) Read not allowed: $L_U = (S, \{I\})$, $L_O = (P, \{A\})$: the compartment test $\{A\} \subseteq \{I\}$ fails, so $L_O 
ot\sqsubseteq L_U$. (4) Write allowed: $L_U = (P, \{I\})$, $L_O = (S, \{I\})$: $P \leq S$ and $\{I\} \subseteq \{I\}$, so $L_U \sqsubseteq L_O$. (5) Write not allowed: $L_U = (S, \{I\})$, $L_O = (P, \{A\})$: the compartment test $\{I\} \subseteq \{A\}$ fails (and $S 
ot\leq P$), so $L_U 
ot\sqsubseteq L_O$.

exam_questions.answer: 2b.1: $C$ and $S$ are incomparable levels, so neither read nor write. Examples: (2) $(S,\{I\})$ reads $(P,\{I\})$; (3) $(S,\{I\})$ cannot read $(P,\{A\})$; (4) $(P,\{I\})$ writes $(S,\{I\})$; (5) $(S,\{I\})$ cannot write $(P,\{A\})$.
